newsitem.title: USA: Sterling collapse brings dollar down with it.
newsitem.headline: Sterling collapse brings dollar down with it.

text.p: The British pound tumbled on Thursday after the Bank of England signalled that British interest rates had risen enough for now, and the dollar fell in sympathy against most leading currencies.
The pound fell to a 10-month low against the dollar and a one-month low against the German mark while the dollar posted its first loss against the mark after surging to a string of eight-year highs.

The British central bank raised its official interest rate to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent, its fourth consecutive monthly increase, but released a statement saying it had no immediate plans for future rate rises, triggering heavy selling in sterling, dealers said.
Higher interest rates tend to raise the value of a currency by boosting the price of assets denominated in that currency.

"When they raised interest rates in the morning, they said basically this was the last one, and that was the reason sterling went down," said Hans Boman, chief spot currency dealer at Swedbank in New York.

The Bank of England also said the sharp rally in sterling, which had risen 16 percent against the German mark in 1997, was pressuring British businesses by making their goods more expensive in global markets.
Currency dealers said investors had been looking for an opportunity to book profits from the pound's rally and seized on the Bank of England's statement.
"When it comes to sterling, we've all been waiting for this for a long time," said Boman.
The pound touched an intraday low at $1.5780, its weakest since last October, before settling at $1.5900 late Thursday, down from $1.6033 late Wednesday.
The dollar fell to 1.8685 marks from 1.8825 marks on Wednesday and to 118.45 Japanese yen from 118.73 yen.
The U.S. currency fell to 1.5303 Swiss francs from 1.5325 Swiss francs on Wednesday and rose to Canadian $1.3882 from C$1.3872.
The dollar tends to trade closely with sterling in currency markets and dealers said the pound's decline also gave investors a chance to book profits from the dollar's sharp rally.

"We saw sterling lead the way up for the dollar for a long time and now that sterling is coming back down, that undermined the dollar against the mark and yen a bit," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal in Chicago.

Investors remain watchful for signs of official efforts to stop the dollar's climb, with 1.90 marks and 120 yen considered trigger points for central banks to intervene in the market and sell dollars, dealers said.

Japan has come under heavy pressure for its growing trade surplus with the United States, which is exacerbated by a strong dollar, while German officials worry that a weak mark will lead to domestic inflation and cheapen the value of the single European currency, the euro, slated for launch in 1999.
"The Bundesbank doesn't want the mark to become a worthless currency and it doesn't want the new euro to become a worthless currency," said Johnson.
Yet investors remained eager to buy dollars on any dips, with the healthy U.S. economy drawing heavy capital flows out of continental Europe and Japan, where economic growth remains feeble.

"A lot of people are happy to see the dollar go down so they can buy it at cheaper levels," said James Powers, vice president for corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
